nameStory: The 'tick-trefoil' name comes from this plant's sneaky seed pods that stick to your clothes and pets just like ticks! The seeds have tiny hooked hairs that grab onto anything that brushes past, earning them the nickname 'beggar's lice.' The 'trefoil' part refers to the three leaflets that make up each leaf, like a clover.
description: Maryland tick-trefoil is a slender perennial wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall in New England's woodlands and edges. It's a member of the legume family, related to beans and peas, with the characteristic three-part leaves and small pink to purple pea-like flowers. The plant has a delicate, wispy appearance with thin stems and small leaflets that give it an almost feathery look from a distance. Like other legumes, it helps enrich soil by fixing nitrogen through special root bacteria.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three small, oval leaflets per leaf with smooth edges and a soft, velvety texture when you rub them gently between your fingers. The leaflets are typically less than an inch long and feel slightly fuzzy underneath.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink to lavender pea-shaped flowers clustered in loose, branching sprays at the top of stems. Each flower is only about 1/4 inch long and has the classic legume flower shape with a banner, wings, and keel.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, jointed seed pods that break apart into triangular segments, each covered in tiny hooked hairs that grab onto clothing with a slight scratching sensation when you try to remove them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, upright stems that branch near the top, creating an open, airy appearance. The plant often leans slightly and may need support from nearby vegetation.

habitat: Look for Maryland tick-trefoil in partially shaded woodlands, forest edges, and clearings throughout New England. It prefers well-drained soils and is often found along woodland paths, in young forests recovering from disturbance, or at the margins where woods meet fields. You'll commonly spot it growing alongside other woodland wildflowers and grasses in areas that get dappled sunlight.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as soft, three-part leaflets that feel distinctly velvety to the touch. Young plants are low and bushy before they send up their flowering stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with small pink-purple flowers appearing in loose clusters from July through August. This is the best time for identification when both flowers and leaves are fully developed.
seasonality.fall: The sticky seed pods mature and become the plant's most noticeable feature, clinging to hikers and their dogs. Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stem remnants. Look for the root crown at soil level where new growth will emerge next spring.

funFact: The hooked seed pods are so effective at hitchhiking that they inspired the invention of Velcro! Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral studied how these 'beggar's lice' seeds stuck to his dog's fur and clothing, leading to his revolutionary hook-and-loop fastener design in the 1940s.
confusionNotes: Maryland tick-trefoil can be tricky to distinguish from its many tick-trefoil cousins, but remember 'small and smooth' - it has smaller leaflets than most relatives and lacks the dense fuzziness of hoary tick-trefoil. The leaflets are also more oval-shaped rather than the broader, rounder leaves of some other species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'Maryland' tick-trefoil, this plant ranges well beyond Maryland throughout the eastern United States. The scientific name 'Desmodium' comes from Greek meaning 'chain' or 'bond,' referring to how the jointed seed pods connect together before breaking apart to spread the seeds.
compareHints: Among New England's tick-trefoils, Maryland tick-trefoil is distinguished by its relatively small, smooth leaflets and delicate overall appearance. Showy tick-trefoil is much taller with larger leaflets, while hoary tick-trefoil has distinctly fuzzy, grayish leaves. Round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil has a prostrate growth habit and rounded leaflets, making Maryland's upright stems and oval leaflets quite different.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, showy tick-trefoil is typically the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most densely packed flower clusters.

Among New England's many ticktrefoils, panicled ticktrefoil stands out with its distinctly narrow, lance-shaped leaflets - much thinner than the broad leaflets of showy tick-trefoil or the rounded leaves of round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil.
Among the tick-trefoils, this is the only one with perfectly round leaflets and a distinctly trailing growth habit.
Among the tick-trefoils, this species stands out for its height and smooth appearance.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, little-leaf stands out for its distinctly smaller leaflets and notably hairy stems.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, perplexed tick-trefoil is most easily confused with tall tick-trefoil, requiring expert examination to separate reliably.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, the toothed variety stands out for its distinctly serrated leaf edges - most other species have smooth or only slightly toothed leaflets.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, hoary tick-trefoil is the gray ghost - its fuzzy, grayish appearance makes it unmistakable.
Among New England's ticktrefoils, sessileleaf is the only one with leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks - all its relatives have obvious leaf stems.
Among the tick-trefoils, stiff tick-trefoil stands out for its rigid, unbending stems - most others like showy tick-trefoil or panicled tick-trefoil have flexible stems that sway easily.
